article_title: Applying a Partially Nested Regression Model to Evaluate the Impact of ASSISTments on Middle School Students' Math Achievement
citation: Huang, C.-W., Feng, M., & Li, L. (2025). Applying a partially nested regression model to evaluate the impact of ASSISTments on middle school students' math achievement. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Virtual comparison group (VCG) construction via NWEA's matching algorithm
description: The VCG approach creates an equivalent virtual comparison for each treatment student: each treatment student was matched with up to 51 real students from NWEA's national MAP test database based on school locale, school-level FRL percentage, test-taking dates, grade level, and pretest scores; aggregated values were treated as a single virtual comparison student. Each virtual student received a comparison criteria level from 0 to 8, with smaller values indicating a closer match. Approximately 89 percent of virtual comparison students were within level 0 to 2.
requirements: Requires access to NWEA's extensive national MAP test database and its matching algorithm, plus treatment-group baseline scores and covariates (locale, FRL, test dates, grade, pretest).
constraints: Matching quality varies: criteria levels ranged from 0 to 8, with 9 virtual students (0.32%) at the loosest level 8; the approach is a proxy for an experimental control group, not random assignment.
examples: In this study, 1,578 virtual comparison students (55.27%) were exact matches at level 0, and the baseline equivalence effect size between groups was -0.03, which the authors say indicates the matching algorithm performed as expected.
key_sources: Huang, C.-W., Feng, M., & Li, L. (2025). Applying a partially nested regression model to evaluate the impact of ASSISTments on middle school students' math achievement. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677665

article_title: Advancing to Completion: Increasing Degree Attainment by Improving Graduation Rates and Closing Gaps for African-American Students
citation: Mary Nguyen, Erin Ward Bibo, and Jennifer Engle. (2012). Advancing to Completion: Increasing degree attainment by improving graduation rates and closing gaps for African-American students. The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org
title: VCU University College model: cohort-based first-year core curriculum with centralized support and proactive advising
description: Virginia Commonwealth University's University College, launched in 2006, is built around "a cohesive core curriculum with a limited set of course options and small class sizes," taught by dedicated cross-disciplinary faculty, with a full-year cohort class. It pairs this with proactive advising — required advisor meetings twice a semester, faculty attendance reporting, and outreach at the first sign of trouble — plus learning, writing, and supplemental instruction centers. After implementation, DFW rates in core courses decreased significantly and retention rose.
requirements: Significant investment and commitment at the highest levels of the institution
Dedicated faculty hired to work across disciplines
Professionally trained advisors tracking student data
constraints: The article attributes the model's success to VCU's context; it reports institutional self-attributions rather than a controlled evaluation
target_learners: First-year undergraduates, including undeclared majors at risk of dropping out
target_learning_goals: First-year course success, retention, and on-time graduation
examples: VCU narrowed its black-white gap from 7.4 points in 2004 to near parity by 2010, with black students graduating at 49.8 percent
The investment in University College was repaid in retention terms in less than three years, per the vice provost
key_sources: Mary Nguyen, Erin Ward Bibo, and Jennifer Engle. (2012). Advancing to Completion: Increasing degree attainment by improving graduation rates and closing gaps for African-American students. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED535504

article_title: Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning
citation: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5
title: Virtual Collaborative Research Institute (VCRI) CSCL environment
description: VCRI is a groupware program designed to support collaborative learning on inquiry tasks and research projects, developed for students from primary to higher education. Students use it to communicate, access information sources, and co-author texts. Its shared tools support three activities of collaborative inquiry: task-related or cognitive activities (Sources-tool, Diagrammer, Debate-tool, Cowriter shared word processor), metacognitive activities (planning and evaluating the inquiry process), and social activities (monitoring the collaborative process and supporting communication, e.g., the synchronous Chat-tool).
requirements: Students work on collaborative inquiry projects over longer periods of time, with teacher access to monitor discussions and texts
constraints: In the reported studies students worked on separate computers in a computer lab and mostly communicated electronically, though they could talk face-to-face
target_learners: Students ranging from primary to higher education; in this study, fifth-year pre-university secondary students
target_learning_goals: Collaborative inquiry: exploring topics, collecting and summarizing sources, discussing, constructing argument diagrams, and co-writing essays
examples: Across the three studies, groups used VCRI for eight 50-minute lessons per inquiry task, producing chat protocols averaging 923 messages per group
key_sources: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5

article_title: Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance
citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3
title: VCRI CSCL environment augmented with representational scripting
description: Virtual Collaborative Research Institute (VCRI) is a groupware application for supporting the collaborative performance of complex learning-tasks, inquiry-tasks and research projects. For this study five tools were augmented with representational scripting: a chat tool for synchronous communication, an Assignment menu with the task description and information sources, a shared Co-writer text processor, an individual Notes tool, and a Status bar awareness tool. Groups had to close each finished phase in the assignment menu, which opened the next phase and delivered the next external representation.
requirements: All students in all conditions had access to these tools and information sources, and were information equivalent
constraints: Only in the matched condition did students receive a new ER matched to the demands of each phase; in the three mismatch conditions the ER did not change
target_learners: secondary education students working in triads
target_learning_goals: collaborative solution of a complex business-economics problem
examples: When group members agreed a part-task was finished they closed that phase, received a new part-task, entered answers in a different Co-writer window, and received an ER
key_sources: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3

article_title: Virtual Chemistry Laboratory: Effect of Constructivist Learning Environment
citation: Zeynep Tatli & Alipasa Ayas. (2012). Virtual Chemistry Laboratory: Effect of Constructivist Learning Environment. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 13(1). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tojde
title: Interactive virtual chemistry laboratory (VCL) software for the 9th-grade chemical changes unit
description: The VCL is interactive software developed for the 'chemical changes' unit of the year-nine chemistry curriculum, built on constructivist theory and the POE strategy. It presents experiments at macro, micro (molecular) and symbolic levels, asks students to record predictions before experimenting, lets them select equipment and assemble experiments themselves, and includes a 'Relate it with Daily Life' button plus safety warnings such as 'The laboratory is kept clean and uncluttered'. Students used it in the information technology class with 2 or 3 students sharing one computer.
requirements: Students record their predictions and data in the VCL before and during the experiment
Teacher starts the experiment with an interesting question and acts as a guide
constraints: In this study EG students were permitted to use VCL software only within chemistry lessons and applications lessons
target_learning_goals: Understanding chemical changes through macro, micro and symbolic representations
Connecting chemistry experiments with daily life
examples: EG students chose the necessary equipment from VCL and established the experiment assembly by themselves; all students in EG performed all the experiments in the unit at least two times
key_sources: Zeynep Tatli & Alipasa Ayas. (2012). Virtual Chemistry Laboratory: Effect of Constructivist Learning Environment. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 13(1). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tojde

article_title: Virtual Chemistry Laboratory: Effect of Constructivist Learning Environment
citation: Zeynep Tatli & Alipasa Ayas. (2012). Virtual Chemistry Laboratory: Effect of Constructivist Learning Environment. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 13(1). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tojde
title: VCL lesson pattern pairing student-centered experiment design with process evaluation
description: Table 2 enumerates the design characteristics the authors built into the VCL: configuration information that inquires into prior knowledge and adapts lab experiences to daily life; student-centered learning through individual or group decision making, open-ended questions during experiments, and interactive experimentation; a teacher role of starting with an interesting question; planning through multimedia with students selecting inventory and equipment; and evaluation by comparing students' prior knowledge with the experiment result at the end. Free science experiments can be done in class or at home using VCL.
requirements: Students select the inventory and all equipment before beginning an experiment
Predictions and data are recorded in the VCL at the predict and observation steps
constraints: The pattern was implemented and observed only for the chemical changes unit in 9th-grade chemistry
target_learning_goals: Constructing knowledge of chemical changes actively
examples: Before starting, VCL asks students to predict about the subject; at the end it supports comparison of prior knowledge with the experiment result
key_sources: Zeynep Tatli & Alipasa Ayas. (2012). Virtual Chemistry Laboratory: Effect of Constructivist Learning Environment. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 13(1). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tojde

article_title: Impacts of Virtual Clinical Trials Simulations on Science Knowledge and Attitudes
citation: Bowling, K. G., Miller, L. M., Patel, R., & Bass, K. M. (2017). Impacts of Virtual Clinical Trials Simulations on Science Knowledge and Attitudes. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 21(7). http://ejse.southwestern.edu
title: Virtual Clinical Trials simulation design grounded in situated learning and possible selves theory
description: The Virtual Clinical Trials simulations are online games recreating published clinical trials (spinal cord injury, teen depression, traumatic brain injury) in which students design trials with career role-play characters. The article states development is "grounded in two theories: Situated learning and Possible Selves", using authentic contexts and career role-play to build knowledge and enrich students' scientific possible selves. Embedded activities require deciding hypotheses, outcome measures, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and conclusions.
requirements: Learning objectives aligned with NGSS and Common Core, developed with high school science teachers
Role-play with clinical trial expert characters providing guidance and feedback
constraints: The third simulation (preclinical rat testing) was excluded from the study
The study was conducted without teacher intervention or led discussion
target_learners: high school Anatomy and Physiology students
target_learning_goals: experimental design concepts within a clinical trial context
examples: Trial 1: Spinal Cord Injury has players help set up a Phase 2 trial testing an electrical device; Trial 2: Teens and Depression has players design a Phase 3 antidepressant trial
key_sources: Bowling, K. G., Miller, L. M., Patel, R., & Bass, K. M. (2017). Impacts of Virtual Clinical Trials Simulations on Science Knowledge and Attitudes. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 21(7). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1187990

article_title: Impacts of Virtual Clinical Trials Simulations on Science Knowledge and Attitudes
citation: Bowling, K. G., Miller, L. M., Patel, R., & Bass, K. M. (2017). Impacts of Virtual Clinical Trials Simulations on Science Knowledge and Attitudes. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 21(7). http://ejse.southwestern.edu
title: Combine game-based simulations with teacher-led reflection and discussion to deepen possible selves and knowledge shifts
description: The article recommends that simulations not be played in isolation: "Incorporating games into a curriculum requires more than just playing a game in isolation." Drawing on Foster and Shah (2016), it argues teacher-led reflection and discussion during and after gameplay could produce greater change in possible selves and knowledge than the no-intervention condition studied here.
requirements: Teacher time and facilitation for reflection and discussion during and after game play
constraints: The study itself was conducted without teacher intervention, so the added benefit of teacher-led discussion was not tested in this research
examples: The authors propose evaluating the simulations with a combined teacher intervention of reflection and discussion as future research
key_sources: Bowling, K. G., Miller, L. M., Patel, R., & Bass, K. M. (2017). Impacts of Virtual Clinical Trials Simulations on Science Knowledge and Attitudes. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 21(7). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1187990

article_title: Microlearning and online simulation-based virtual consultation training module for the undergraduate medical curriculum - a preliminary evaluation.
citation: Liew Siaw Cheok, Tan Maw Pin, Breen Emer, Krishnan Kuhan, Sivarajah Inthirani, Raviendran Nivashinie, Aung Thidar, Nimir Amal, Pallath Vinod. (2023). Microlearning and online simulation-based virtual consultation training module for the undergraduate medical curriculum – a preliminary evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04777-1
title: The module's instructional design integrated competency-based medical education, the 4CID model, and constructive alignment under Kern's six-step model
description: The article frames its virtual consultation module with a design framework combining competency-based medical education with Kern's six-step curriculum development model. The "4CID model in SBE encompasses the following: (i) structuring learning tasks, (ii) offering supportive information, (iii) providing procedural information, and (iv) focusing on part-task practice". Constructive alignment consolidated teaching–learning and assessment strategies with the VC competencies, and the module was implemented and evaluated as Kern's steps 4, 5, and 6.
requirements: Outcome competencies must be explicitly articulated (derived from the VC-EPA competency framework) so syllabus content and learning opportunities can be aligned to them
constraints: The article describes the framework as applied to a pilot module for senior clinical students; transfer to junior students or other curricula is stated as requiring further work
target_learners: Year 4 and 5 clinical medical students and fresh graduates not yet in housemanship or residency
target_learning_goals: Virtual consultation competencies: initiating a VC, history-taking and communication, observational examination, patient management, ethics and professionalism, and concluding a VC
examples: Steps 4–6 of Kern's model operationalised as a six-week module: microlearning videos and quizzes in weeks 1–2, facilitated simulated-patient sessions in weeks 3–5, and pre/post DOVCS assessment in weeks 1 and 6
key_sources: Liew Siaw Cheok, Tan Maw Pin, Breen Emer, Krishnan Kuhan, Sivarajah Inthirani, Raviendran Nivashinie, Aung Thidar, Nimir Amal, Pallath Vinod. (2023). Microlearning and online simulation-based virtual consultation training module for the undergraduate medical curriculum – a preliminary evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04777-1

article_title: Virtual classroom proficiency-based progression for robotic surgery training (VROBOT): a randomised, prospective, cross-over, effectiveness study.
citation: Nathan Arjun, Patel Sonam, Georgi Maria, Fricker Monty, Asif Aqua, Ng Alexander, Mullins William, Hang Man Kien, Light Alexander, Nathan Senthil, Francis Nader, Kelly John, Collins Justin, Sridhar Ashwin. (2022). Virtual classroom proficiency-based progression for robotic surgery training (VROBOT): a randomised, prospective, cross-over, effectiveness study. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-022-01467-w
title: Virtual classroom training (VCT) studio with BARCO weConnect remote connectivity for robotic surgery teaching
description: The virtual classroom is "a studio with multiple audio–visual inputs to which participants can connect remotely via the BARCO weConnect platform". The studio provides a live feed of attending participants and a dual camera set-up giving students both close-up and wide views of instructors, who use the WeConnect interactive digital whiteboard. An expert high-volume robotic surgeon hosts the session with an instructor-to-student ratio of 1:12, combining computer-based learning with concurrent expert instruction and live interactive feedback.
requirements: Requires the BARCO weConnect platform and a studio with multiple audio-visual inputs and a dual camera set-up
Requires an expert instructor host; the study used an instructor-to-student ratio of 1:12
constraints: The authors state applicability to smaller centres, where continued access to VCT technology and robotic simulators may be challenging, is not known
target_learners: Novice surgical trainees with no prior robotic surgery experience
target_learning_goals: Basic robotic surgical technical skills such as camera control, instrument handling, docking, and suturing tasks
examples: In the VROBOT study, participants connected remotely to a UCL studio-hosted session while undertaking the FRS curriculum on the daVinci simulator
key_sources: Nathan Arjun, Patel Sonam, Georgi Maria, Fricker Monty, Asif Aqua, Ng Alexander, Mullins William, Hang Man Kien, Light Alexander, Nathan Senthil, Francis Nader, Kelly John, Collins Justin, Sridhar Ashwin. (2022). Virtual classroom proficiency-based progression for robotic surgery training (VROBOT): a randomised, prospective, cross-over, effectiveness study. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-022-01467-w

article_title: Virtual care is growing, but who will train upcoming learners to practice it?
citation: Lee J, Kron F. (2022). Virtual care is growing, but who will train upcoming learners to practice it? Med Educ. 2022;56(12):1155-1157. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14934
title: Institutions should form virtual care advisory committees to determine educationally enriching VC practices
description: Because practitioners may be enthusiastic teachers with established methods but are not necessarily inclined toward or experienced with pedagogic innovation, and innovation is not within any one individual's purview in a large healthcare system, the commentary underscores "the need for institutions to form VC advisory committees to discern the most efficient and educationally enriching VC practices and procedures". Educators should balance research with organisational constraints and practitioner needs.
requirements: Institutional-level structures are needed because pedagogic innovation in VC exceeds the purview of individual practitioners.
constraints: Educators must balance research evidence with organisational constraints and the needs of practitioners in their home institution.
target_learners: Health professions learners in institutions delivering virtual care
target_learning_goals: Institutional design of efficient and educationally enriching virtual care training practices
examples: The commentary proposes advisory committees as the institutional mechanism for discerning VC practices and procedures.
key_sources: Lee J, Kron F. (2022). Virtual care is growing, but who will train upcoming learners to practice it? Med Educ. 2022;56(12):1155-1157. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14934
